subtype: Trusting an influencer like a friend [Receiver]
passage:
You keep saying that boy on your phone is like a friend, Santosh. Let me tell you about my friend on the radio.
I was fifteen. Every night at nine, a woman called Sunita Kiran read letters from girls like me on the radio. She laughed at our jokes, she remembered names, she said, "My dear listeners, you are my family." I felt she was talking only to me.
One night she said she used Chandan Glow powder every day and so should I. I took my whole Diwali money to the market and bought three tins.
My face broke out. When I wrote to her, "from Minakshi, your listener", I got a printed card back. Later my cousin at the radio station told me the powder company paid for that whole half-hour.
I still liked her voice. But I stopped buying what she said.

qa.q: How many tins of powder did young Minakshi buy?
qa.a: Minakshi bought three tins with her whole Diwali money.

qa.q: Why did fifteen-year-old Minakshi trust the powder advice so easily?
qa.a: Minakshi felt that Sunita Kiran was talking only to her, like family, so she believed the advice came from a friend and did not question it.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Minakshi listened?
qa.a: Receiving only a printed card and then learning the company paid for the half-hour showed her the friendly voice was also selling.

qa.q: How might Sunita Kiran's show have looked to the powder company?
qa.a: To the company, the warm, family-like show was a way to reach girls who trusted the host, which is exactly why they paid for it.

grounding: A woman tells Santosh how at fifteen she trusted a friendly radio host like family and bought a product that turned out to be paid promotion.

subtype: Trusting an influencer like a friend [Receiver]
passage:
It was 11:40 at night and the discount code ran out at midnight.
Vinita had watched Pari's videos every day for a year. Pari talked about exam stress and her own acne, and once she replied to Vinita's comment with a heart. So when Pari said, "Guys, this serum changed my skin, I'd never lie to you," Vinita believed her.
The serum cost 1,200 rupees, almost all the money she had kept from her birthday. The phone was at 3 percent.
Aditi, sharing the room, leaned over. "Why is there a tiny 'paid partnership' line under the name?"
Vinita hadn't seen it. She felt her face go hot, like she'd been caught out by someone she trusted.
"She still might like it," Aditi said. "But she's also paid for it."
The phone died at 11:52. Vinita decided to read some reviews in the morning.

qa.q: What line did Aditi notice under Pari's name?
qa.a: Aditi noticed a tiny "paid partnership" line under the name.

qa.q: How did Vinita feel when she saw the paid partnership line?
qa.a: Vinita felt embarrassed and a little betrayed; her face went hot, as if someone she trusted had caught her out.

qa.q: What was the turning point that slowed Vinita down?
qa.a: Aditi pointing out the paid partnership line, and then the phone dying, gave Vinita a pause to check reviews in the morning instead of buying under the midnight deadline.

qa.q: How might Aditi see Pari differently from Vinita?
qa.a: Aditi has not built a bond with Pari, so Aditi can see both sides: Pari might like the serum and is also being paid to sell it.

grounding: A teenage girl trusts a creator like a friend and nearly buys a paid product before midnight, until Aditi, who shares the room, notices the sponsorship label.
